heading: PROPHET SULAYMĀN (AS)
title: WISDOM, GRATITUDE & THE TRUST OF POWER
themes: Tawḥīd • Knowledge • Mercy • Verification • Consultation • Justice • Gratitude • Humility
scope: 8 CONNECTED STORIES | 12 INTERACTIVE MISSIONS | 15 SELECTED QUR’ANIC PASSAGES
introduction: Volume Seventeen follows the world of Prophet Dāwūd (AS). His son, Prophet Sulaymān (AS), received knowledge and extraordinary favours by Allah’s permission. The Qur’an tells us of his understanding in a case of judgment (21:78–79), the speech of birds and warning of an ant (27:16–19), the hoopoe’s report of a people worshipping the sun (27:20–28), the ruler of Sabaʾ and her eventual submission to Allah (27:29–44), the wind and jinn made subject to him by Allah (34:12–13), and a lesson concerning the unseen in the account of his death (34:14). The purpose is Tawḥīd, responsibility and gratitude—not admiration for power as entertainment.

Our fictional companions Imaan, Akhlaq, Mohsin, Mohsina, Salaam, Salamah, Dadi Jaan, Sheikh Uncle and Sir Zameer prepare a “Small Voices, Big Responsibility” exhibition at their academy. Their decisions illuminate limited ethical applications without entering, reconstructing or dramatizing sacred Prophetic history. Qur’anic narratives and fictional family events must always be clearly labelled.

stories.title: The Exhibition with an Empty Corner
stories.subtitle: Knowledge is entrusted to us; welcome smaller voices

blocks.text: The invitation to Sheikh Uncle’s Academy arrived on a bright Saturday morning. It announced a new exhibition: SMALL VOICES, BIG RESPONSIBILITY. Akhlaq read the words twice and laughed. “How can a small voice be important? Surely the loudest person wins the prize.” Imaan put down her breakfast. “Maybe that is exactly what we are meant to discover.”

At school, Sir Zameer gave each team a table and asked them to arrange a display about using gifts wisely. Mohsin immediately suggested a large model building. Mohsina wanted a corner for younger pupils to share ideas, but her suggestion was lost beneath several louder voices. The team spent nearly an hour discussing materials and did not ask the younger pupils what they needed.

Dadi Jaan visited with a Qur’an and pointed them towards the account of Dāwūd and Sulaymān. Allah granted them knowledge, and the Qur’an speaks of Sulaymān’s special understanding in a matter of judgment. “These were gifts from Allah,” she reminded the children. “No competition can earn Prophethood, and no school project can recreate these events.”

Imaan looked at the nearly finished display. It was splendid—and impossible for the youngest children to reach. She invited two younger pupils to look at it. One quietly asked whether the labels could be placed lower. The other asked for a place to sit while listening. Akhlaq first felt embarrassed. Then he moved the labels and fetched a stool.

The next morning the empty corner had become the most welcoming part of the exhibition. There was no magic and no dramatic announcement. The team simply understood that knowledge and responsibility belonged together. As the visitors entered, Akhlaq wrote a new question on the poster: WHO HAVE WE NOT LISTENED TO YET?

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Knowledge that benefits people begins with attentive responsibility.

stories.title: The Message from the Garden
stories.subtitle: Mercy toward small creatures and humble gratitude

blocks.text: A few days later the academy garden was being prepared for a family visit. Akhlaq was moving an empty flowerpot when Mohsina called out, “Watch your feet!” A small line of ants was crossing the path beside the tap. Akhlaq stepped back, surprised that anyone had noticed them.

“Why should we change our plan for a few ants?” another student asked. Mohsina pointed to the plants. “We can move our things without disturbing them. It costs almost nothing to be careful.” The students placed the pots elsewhere and asked their teacher for guidance about protecting the garden without touching wild creatures.

During the lesson, Sheikh Uncle read from Sūrat al-Naml. The Qur’an describes an ant warning other ants as Sulaymān’s forces approached. Allah had enabled Sulaymān to understand what was said, and he responded by smiling and praying to be grateful for Allah’s favours and to perform righteous deeds. Akhlaq was amazed. He asked whether he could learn to speak with ants if he passed enough missions in the app.
“No,” said Sheikh Uncle. “That was an extraordinary favour Allah gave His Prophet. Our mission is different. We can practise consideration and gratitude in ordinary life.”

Later, Mohsin suggested displaying a warning sign near the garden path. “Please watch where you step,” it read. Imaan added a small sentence: “Allah’s creatures are not obstacles in our way.” At home Akhlaq remembered how quickly he had dismissed something small. He thanked Allah for his ability to notice and for friends who had reminded him to be gentle.

As the children checked their exhibition notebook, a folded page slipped out. Someone had written an accusation about a missing school resource. The next lesson would require much more than careful footsteps.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Mercy includes noticing small and vulnerable creatures, and gratitude produces action.

stories.title: The Missing Page of the Report
stories.subtitle: Verify news before repeating or acting

blocks.text: The folded page said that someone had deliberately taken a box of art supplies from the classroom. It gave a pupil’s name but no explanation. Akhlaq felt a rush of excitement. At last the exhibition had a real mystery. He began composing a message for the class group.

Imaan caught his hand before he pressed send. “How do we know it is true?” she asked. Akhlaq pointed to the handwriting. “Someone wrote it. That means something.” Mohsin shook his head. “It means someone wrote it. We still need the truth.” They took the note to Sir Zameer instead of sharing it.

In their Qur’an lesson, they studied the hoopoe’s report to Prophet Sulaymān (AS). The hoopoe brought news from Sabaʾ. Sulaymān did not simply treat the report as permission to act on every claim: the Qur’an records that he intended to examine its truth. Sir Zameer explained that children were learning a limited communication lesson from the account; they were not imitating a Prophet’s authority or investigating each other.

The teacher checked the store records. The supplies had been moved for a supervised activity. A label had been misplaced, and a pupil had assumed the worst. Sir Zameer settled the matter privately. Nobody needed to become a public suspect.

Akhlaq deleted the message draft. “I nearly turned a sentence into a story,” he admitted. “And a story into an accusation,” Imaan added. Together they made three cards for the exhibition: WHO SAID IT? HOW DO WE KNOW? WHO CAN HELP SAFELY?
Before leaving, Mohsina found another note tucked behind the report. It contained a question for their next exhibit: CAN A MESSAGE BE FIRM AND STILL RESPECTFUL?

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: When news may harm someone, verify and seek trustworthy help rather than spreading it.

For their fourth activity, the children had to write a letter inviting another class to the exhibition. Akhlaq drafted a dramatic message: “You MUST come! Our display is the BEST!” Mohsin liked it. Imaan did not. “If we want them to learn with us, why are we shouting at them?”

Dadi Jaan invited them to read the Qur’anic account of the message sent by Prophet Sulaymān (AS) to the ruler of Sabaʾ. The account includes an opening in Allah’s name and a call away from arrogance and towards submission. The Qur’an also describes the people of Sabaʾ worshipping the sun, and later the ruler’s submission to Allah. Dadi made the distinction clear: this was a Prophetic call to Tawḥīd, not merely a lesson in polite handwriting.

The children rewrote their own invitation. They greeted the other class, explained the purpose of the exhibition and invited honest questions. They left out the boastful claims. “Would you like to visit and share an idea about responsibility?” the new letter asked.

When the guests arrived, one child noticed that the exhibit about gratitude had no practical activity. Akhlaq nearly argued that the display was already perfect. He remembered that inviting a person to contribute meant accepting that they might see what he had missed. Instead, he asked how they could improve it. Together they added a thank-you card station.

On the walk home, Salaam observed that respectful words mattered, but truthful intentions mattered even more. Akhlaq tucked the first draft into the recycling bin. He had learned that firm conviction did not require arrogance, and a courteous letter was worth little unless the writer was ready to act fairly.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Words should serve truth and guidance rather than pride.

stories.title: The Decision Nobody Should Make Alone
stories.subtitle: Consultation, careful judgment and limits of influence

blocks.text: A week before the public exhibition, heavy rain damaged the paper signs outside the academy. There was room in the budget for only one improvement: replace the signs, or make the entrance easier to use for visitors needing a clear path. The team split almost at once.

Mohsin wanted the signs because they would make the display look impressive. Mohsina pointed to a crowded doorway and asked how someone with a mobility aid would enter. Akhlaq was impatient. “I am team captain today. I can decide.” Sir Zameer answered, “A captain’s duty is not to end discussion before hearing it.”

In class they revisited the Qur’an’s account of the ruler of Sabaʾ consulting her leading people after receiving Sulaymān’s letter. Her decision belonged to a specific historical setting; the children were not being asked to treat her every action as religious guidance. Rather, they could recognise that serious decisions deserve information and counsel. They also remembered that Allah gave Sulaymān understanding in a judgment described in Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ.

With the teacher supervising, each student described the needs of visitors. They assessed safety first, then cost. The class chose a clear entrance and made simple handwritten signs using materials already available. No child was asked to solve a safety issue independently.

The visitors arrived through an uncluttered doorway. Even Mohsin agreed that the decision had been better because everyone spoke. Akhlaq wrote on the team log: LEADERSHIP IS NOT THE RIGHT TO STOP LISTENING. Then he crossed out “team captain” beside his name and replaced it with “team member responsible for checking the entrance.” He liked the new title more.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Wise responsibility includes counsel, evidence and concern for those affected.

stories.title: The Gift That Could Not Buy an Answer
stories.subtitle: Integrity when offered rewards and advantages

blocks.text: An unfamiliar visitor came to the exhibition planning meeting with a basket of treats for the team. He offered to sponsor the event if his family business logo appeared as the main title. The children loved the idea of a larger display. Akhlaq began to imagine colourful banners and prizes for everyone.

Sir Zameer thanked the visitor and explained that any sponsorship would need school approval and clear conditions. The exhibition was for education, not for selling praise. He asked the children to think about the difference between receiving an ordinary gift and allowing a reward to change an honest decision.

The lesson returned to Sūrat al-Naml, where the ruler of Sabaʾ sent a gift and Sulaymān responded that what Allah had given him was better. In that context, he was not accepting a worldly offering in place of the truth to which he called them. Sheikh Uncle reminded everyone that the Qur’anic incident was far greater than a school sponsorship choice; the analogy here concerned integrity, not the authority of a Prophet.

The school considered the proposal and chose not to rename its learning exhibition. Instead, the children wrote a polite thank-you note. “We appreciate your generosity,” it said, “but our learning goals must remain clear.”

At home, Imaan asked Akhlaq what he had wanted most. He answered, “To win a prize for the brightest display.” She asked whether the lessons would have become more truthful with a brighter banner. Akhlaq smiled reluctantly. “No. Perhaps the plain signs are enough.”

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: A reward should not purchase our honesty or change what we know is right.

stories.title: The Wonderful Result and the Quiet Prayer
stories.subtitle: Success is a test of gratitude, not a trophy

blocks.text: The family exhibition opened at last. Visitors stopped at the garden-care station, read the fairness cards and listened to children explain how they had revised their decisions. The teachers thanked the team. By noon they had received more appreciative notes than they expected.

Mohsin carried a stack of cards proudly. “We are famous!” he announced. Akhlaq almost agreed, but saw Mohsina quietly cleaning a spilled cup of water. Their display would not be useful if somebody slipped while reading it. He fetched a cloth and helped.

When Dadi Jaan joined them, she reminded the children that Sūrat al-Naml describes Sulaymān recognising a remarkable favour from Allah as a test: would he be grateful? It was an extraordinary event in his life, not an achievement unlocked by a game. “Success can make a person forget the people who helped,” she said. “Or it can make them more thankful.”

The team decided to thank the caretaker, teachers and younger pupils who had offered feedback. They also used leftover paper to create simple take-home cards for families. Nobody received a trophy for the most sincere heart; there was no way to measure such a thing.

At night Akhlaq opened his notebook to write that the exhibition had been a success. He paused, then added: “Alḥamdulillāh. I want the learning to keep changing what I do.” On the next line he wrote the name of one person he still needed to thank. That seemed a better ending than a photograph of himself holding a medal.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Success is an opportunity to thank Allah and serve others.

stories.title: What Power Cannot Know
stories.subtitle: Humility before the unseen and practical gratitude

blocks.text: On the last day, the school library displayed a final question: WHAT CAN GREAT POWER NEVER GIVE A HUMAN BEING? Some pupils answered “more strength.” Others said “more money.” Akhlaq guessed “a bigger army,” thinking of the extraordinary favours given to Prophet Sulaymān (AS).

Sheikh Uncle read carefully from Sūrat Sabaʾ. Allah had subjected the wind and some jinn to Sulaymān by His permission. Yet the Qur’an’s account of his death showed that the jinn did not possess knowledge of the unseen. The children did not recreate the event or turn it into a frightening picture. They read the verse and discussed only what the evidence established.

Dadi Jaan added that the Qur’an rejects false accusations against Sulaymān concerning disbelief and magic. No one should treat his Prophethood as a fantasy about spells or secret powers. Human knowledge is limited; Allah alone possesses complete knowledge of the unseen.

The class prepared its final display using four plain words: KNOWLEDGE, MERCY, TRUTH, GRATITUDE. Each family chose one useful practice rather than a public promise about feelings. Mohsin wanted to check information before repeating it. Mohsina wanted to keep the path safe for smaller visitors. Imaan chose to ask for counsel before difficult decisions. Akhlaq chose to thank Allah and act more carefully when he received praise.

When the building emptied, the little compass from their earlier journeys lay inside its case. It had never needed to open a door. The children now knew that the next direction was an ordinary decision made with sincere guidance. Dadi Jaan placed a new card beside it: ANOTHER STORY OF PROPHETHOOD IS WAITING. The children smiled. The journey of ʿIBRAH Junior would continue.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: No human power replaces Tawḥīd, humility or awareness of our limits.

synthesis.text: What we learned from the Qur’an

Sulaymān (AS), son of Dāwūd (AS), was honoured with knowledge, judgment, Prophethood and remarkable favours granted by Allah. He understood the warning of an ant, prayed to be thankful, examined a report from the hoopoe, and called the people of Sabaʾ to worship Allah alone. Their ruler eventually affirmed submission to Allah. When Sulaymān saw an extraordinary favour, he treated it as a test of gratitude. The account of his death shows that the jinn did not know the unseen. These are not magic powers or achievements children should attempt to reproduce.
Eight lessons to carry into daily life
Use knowledge to help, not to belittle.
Notice the small and vulnerable; kindness is not reserved for the powerful.
Thank Allah for gifts and ask Him for help doing good.
Verify news before repeating it or harming someone’s reputation.
Speak respectfully while remaining truthful about your faith.
Consult responsible adults and the people affected by ordinary decisions.
Refuse rewards that would make you dishonest or unjust.
Remember that success is a test, and only Allah knows the unseen completely.
A moment to reflect — family conversation

Ask one optional question at a time: “Who is not being heard?”, “What information should we check?”, “What can we do to care for an animal safely?”, “Did praise help us become more grateful?”, “When should we seek an adult’s help?” Never demand private confession or rank children by spiritual worth.
